title: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis. Claude can now use desktop apps on Team and Enterprise plans. Anthropic’s IPO closes at $93.5 billion as its shares slip 8.5% on day two, GPT-6.2 reaches Microsoft Copilot, OpenAI tightens defences against model copying, and UK MPs call for an AI law.
summary: Levent Alpöge of Anthropic released a Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis found with Claude; independent mathematicians compiled it, but a full check and a readable write-up are still to come. Anthropic switched on computer use in beta for Claude Team and Enterprise, off by default and controlled by owners. Its IPO closed at about $93.5 billion gross, plus a $26 billion sale to seven chip and cloud partners, while the shares closed Friday at $88.91, down 8.5%. Microsoft is rolling out GPT-6.2 Sol in Copilot, including Word, Excel and PowerPoint, with Astra in Cowork and Studio. OpenAI says attacks that recover GPT-6.2 Astra’s hidden reasoning succeed 0.2% of the time in its tests, down from 54.0%. Two UK parliamentary committees called for an AI bill and a regulator.
uncertainty: The Riemann proof has passed independent compilation, not the full comparator check, and there is no human-readable proof yet; Anthropic had not responded to Nature’s request for comment when it reported. Computer use details are from Anthropic’s help pages and are rolling out gradually. IPO proceeds are Anthropic’s figures; the day-two close and valuation are Reuters’. Copilot availability varies by region, organisation and admin settings. Distillation figures are from OpenAI’s own tests. The UK reports are committee recommendations, not government policy.

stories.theme: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis; the computer-checked proof passes early checks, but no one can read it yet
stories.changed: On 20 November 2026 Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, released a four-page note saying: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.” The hypothesis, posed in 1859, is about how prime numbers are spread out and is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems. Alpöge did not release a full written proof. He released a version written in Lean, a programming language in which a computer checks every step of a proof. Scientific American reports that independent mathematicians, including MIT’s Andrew Sutherland, compiled the Lean code themselves without problems, while a further “comparator” check, which confirms the code proves the real statement and does not quietly redefine anything, was still pending when it reported. Some experts are critical: Nature quotes number theorist Andrew Granville calling the note “garbled” and questioning its timing, a day after Anthropic’s stock market debut. Alpöge wrote that the cynical view of the timing is false. The same day, Stanford’s Ravi Vakil posted a separate, entirely human proof of the generalised hypothesis by postdoc Alessandro Masullo, which has not been machine-checked, TechCrunch reports.
stories.matters: If it holds, an AI model helped settle the most famous open problem in mathematics. It also shows a new kind of result: work a computer has checked line by line that no person yet understands.
stories.imply: A program that compiles is not the same as an explanation. The Clay Institute’s prize needs a published, peer-reviewed proof that survives two years of scrutiny, and mathematicians say humans still have to understand the argument. The same gap appears at work when AI output passes tests nobody can explain.
uses: When AI writes code, formulas or analysis for you, add an automatic check you trust, such as tests or a reconciliation, before you rely on it.
Ask for a plain-language explanation alongside any AI result that passes a check, and do not ship what nobody on the team can explain.
Before quoting a big AI claim to clients or managers, wait for independent experts, not just the company that made the claim.
stories.example: A finance analyst lets an AI rebuild a pricing model, runs it against last year’s actual figures as an automatic check, then asks the AI to explain each changed formula before presenting it.
stories.audience: Researchers, engineers and analysts who use AI for hard technical work, and anyone judging bold AI claims.
stories.watch: The comparator and other independent checks, a human-readable write-up from Alpöge, what Anthropic says officially, and how the human proof by Masullo fares.

source.title: Scientific American: The AI Riemann hypothesis proof is almost certainly true, independent mathematicians attest, 20 November 2026
source.quote: The Lean proof has been compiled and independently rechecked by the Lean kernel with only the three standard axioms.

stories.theme: Claude can now use desktop apps for Team and Enterprise customers, in beta and off until an owner turns it on
stories.changed: On 20 November 2026 Anthropic made computer use available in beta on Claude Team and Enterprise plans, rolling out to organisations gradually. Claude sees the user’s screen and clicks and types in the desktop apps the user allows, from Claude Desktop on macOS 14 or later and Windows, and from Claude on the web or mobile if a computer with Claude Desktop open is reachable. It is off by default: only an Owner or Primary Owner can turn it on, under Organization settings > Capabilities, and the new unified Chat and Cowork experience must be on. Admins can restrict it to specific apps or block it through device management, and on Enterprise limit it to certain roles. It does not work in separate Cowork tasks or Claude Code, and organisations with HIPAA-ready, CMEK, FERPA or K-12 settings, or Zero Data Retention for Claude Code, cannot use it. Anthropic’s setup page warns there is no sandbox between Claude and the user’s apps, that it can open, change or delete files outside connected folders, and that screenshots are saved with the chat. Turning it off can take about an hour to reach each user.
stories.matters: Google’s new Gemini computer use on Mac is for personal accounts only. Claude’s version is aimed at company accounts with admin controls, so IT teams now have a real decision to make about letting an AI drive work computers.
stories.imply: Admin settings help, but the risks are on Anthropic’s own page: a web page or email on screen could steer Claude, and folder limits and read-only marks do not apply. Start with a small group, a short list of apps and no access to finance or HR systems.
uses: Let Claude move data between an old desktop tool with no connector and a spreadsheet.
Have it work through a repetitive set-up task in a desktop app, such as creating the same project in several tools.
Pilot it with one team on non-sensitive apps and review the saved screenshots weekly.
stories.example: An IT admin turns computer use on for a five-person operations role only, allows just Excel and the company’s shipping desktop app, and asks the team to report any action Claude took that they did not expect.
stories.audience: IT and security admins on Claude Team and Enterprise, operations teams with desktop-only tools.
stories.watch: When the rollout reaches your organisation, whether Anthropic adds a sandbox, and how often prompt-style tricks on screen cause unintended actions.

source.title: Anthropic: Set up computer use for Team and Enterprise plans (Claude Help Center), 20 November 2026
source.quote: Computer use has no sandbox between Claude and a user's applications.

stories.theme: Anthropic’s IPO closes at $93.5 billion with the extra shares sold, and its stock falls 8.5% on day two to $88.91
stories.changed: On 20 November 2026 Anthropic closed its IPO. It had sold 980 million shares at $83 on Wednesday for $81.3 billion, CNBC reports; then underwriters bought all 147 million extra shares they had an option on, taking the total to 1,127,000,000 shares at $83, for gross proceeds of about $93.5 billion, of which about $91.6 billion went to Anthropic and the rest to existing shareholders who sold. It also closed a separate $26.0 billion sale of 313,253,007 Class N shares at the same $83 price to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC Partners. Together that is about $119.5 billion before fees, the company says. On the stock market it was a rough second day: Reuters reports the shares closed at $88.91, 8.5% below Thursday’s $97.17 close (they had opened on Thursday at $111.50) and not far from the $83 IPO price, during a broad tech sell-off in which Nvidia fell about 14%. Reuters puts Anthropic’s fully diluted value at about $1.6 trillion, and says Morgan Stanley, which was tasked with stabilising the shares, closed the position meant to do that. Options trading on the stock is due to start next week.
stories.matters: The money is now in the bank: about $91.6 billion from the IPO plus $26 billion from chip and cloud partners, which pays for the compute behind Claude. The falling share price shows investors are cautious about AI spending, not that anything changed for Claude users.
stories.imply: A large part of the new money comes from the companies Anthropic buys chips and cloud from, which ties them closer together. Expect more share price swings once options trading starts; it says little about the product you use.
uses: If your company plans around Claude, note that Anthropic now has fresh cash for capacity, and ask your account team what that means for limits.
Finance teams: use Anthropic’s release, not headlines, for the exact proceeds figures.
Keep tracking how AI vendors are valued; it affects their pricing and the pressure to make money from customers.
stories.example: A CFO preparing a board note quotes the $93.5 billion gross IPO figure from Anthropic’s release and adds that the stock closed day two at $88.91, rather than mixing figures from different reports.
stories.audience: Finance teams, investors and companies that rely on Claude.
stories.watch: Where the shares settle once options start, Anthropic’s first quarterly results as a public company, and whether OpenAI goes ahead with a listing next year.

source.title: Anthropic: Closing of initial public offering and concurrent private placement, 20 November 2026
source.quote: The aggregate gross proceeds from the offering, before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses, were approximately $93.5 billion, of which approximately $91.6 billion was received by Anthropic.

stories.theme: OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Sol is rolling out in Microsoft Copilot, including Word, Excel and PowerPoint; GPT-6.2 Astra comes to Copilot Cowork and Studio
stories.changed: On 20 November 2026 Microsoft said OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Sol and GPT-6.2 Astra are joining the models available in Microsoft Copilot. GPT-6.2 Sol is rolling out worldwide to eligible users in Copilot Chat, Copilot Cowork, Copilot Studio and Copilot in Excel, PowerPoint and Word. GPT-6.2 Astra, the heavier model, is rolling out in Copilot Cowork and Copilot Studio; users in Microsoft’s Frontier programme can also use it in Copilot Chat and the Office apps. Microsoft says its Work IQ layer grounds both models in your files, meetings, chats and business data, within the permissions each person already has. Admins control access through the Microsoft 365 admin center, and availability can vary by region and organisation. OpenAI launched the two models on 17 November.
stories.matters: Copilot users get OpenAI’s newest models inside the documents and spreadsheets they already use, three days after OpenAI launched them.
stories.imply: Which model you get depends on your admin, your region and the app. Copilot only sees what you are allowed to see, so messy file permissions will show up in answers.
uses: Use Sol in Word or PowerPoint for everyday drafting from your own files and meeting notes.
Hand longer multi-step jobs, such as a research brief across several documents, to Astra in Copilot Cowork.
Admins: decide which model each group gets and check file permissions before widening access.
stories.example: A consultant asks Copilot Cowork, running GPT-6.2 Astra, to gather last quarter’s client meeting notes and spreadsheets into a ten-slide review deck, then checks every figure before sending.
stories.audience: Microsoft 365 Copilot users and admins, consultants and analysts who live in Office apps.
stories.watch: When Astra reaches all users in the Office apps, and whether your organisation’s admins switch the new models on.

stories.theme: OpenAI tightens defences against rivals copying its models, and GPT-6.2 now drops hidden reasoning when you edit an earlier message
stories.changed: On 20 November 2026 OpenAI described how it fights “adversarial distillation”: someone using a model’s answers without permission to train a copy that lacks its safety protections, for example a copy that will help with cyberattacks the original would refuse. OpenAI says it combines red-team testing, training, classifiers, API limits and investigations, and puts special effort into protecting the model’s hidden working, its chain of thought. In its own adaptive test, the share of attacks that recovered that hidden reasoning fell from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra. For developers there are practical changes: with GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, a model’s reasoning is tied to the conversation that produced it, so if an earlier message is rewritten, the API drops the reasoning that followed; older model families cannot read GPT-6.2’s reasoning. OpenAI also says it closed a pathway that could have exposed another user’s encrypted reasoning, enforces against networks of accounts, and shares warning signs with other AI companies.
stories.matters: Safety rules only work if they cannot be copied away. For businesses building on OpenAI, the change to how reasoning is kept affects cost and results in multi-step agents.
stories.imply: The 54.0% and 0.2% figures are from OpenAI’s own tests. Agents that edit or rewrite earlier messages in a conversation will lose reasoning and may cost more; OpenAI advises adding new turns instead.
uses: Developers: change agents to append new messages rather than editing earlier ones when using GPT-6.2.
Security teams: ask your AI vendors how they detect bulk scraping of their models through your accounts.
Review API keys shared across teams, since OpenAI says it enforces against whole networks of accounts it links to distillation.
stories.example: A developer finds her support agent rewrites the first message on every turn, switches it to add a new message instead, and keeps the model’s earlier reasoning in play.
stories.audience: Developers on the OpenAI API, security and trust teams, AI policy watchers.
stories.watch: Whether other labs publish similar figures, and any public case of a distilled model being used for harm.

source.title: OpenAI: Combatting adversarial distillation, 20 November 2026
source.quote: The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

stories.theme: Two UK parliamentary committees in one week call for an AI law and a regulator with powers to pause or block risky systems
stories.changed: On 18 November 2026 the House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee published “Guardrails for growth: AI safety and security”. It asks for an AI Safety and Security Bill in the next session of Parliament and a new regulator, separate from the AI Security Institute, with legal powers to require independent checks of safety claims, pause high-risk training and testing, delay or prohibit deployment, and suspend services when risks cannot be controlled. It lists ten gaps, including mandatory incident reporting and protection for whistleblowers. On 20 November the Joint Committee on Human Rights published the government’s response to its own report, which called for a risk-based AI bill, one independent regulator, and a duty to tell people when AI that can significantly affect them is being used. Its chair, Alex Sobel MP, said the committee is not seeing a sense of urgency from the government.
stories.matters: These are recommendations, not law. But two cross-party committees landing in the same place gives future UK rules a likely shape: incident reporting, independent testing and disclosure when AI makes significant decisions.
stories.imply: Nothing changes for UK businesses today. Companies that deploy AI in hiring, lending or customer decisions should expect disclosure and incident-reporting duties to come up in any bill.
uses: Start a simple log of AI incidents and near misses now; it is the most common demand in these reports.
List where your company uses AI to make decisions about people, and whether those people are told.
Check your whistleblowing policy covers concerns about AI systems.
stories.example: An HR director at a UK retailer adds a line to job adverts saying AI helps screen applications, and sets up a form for staff to report AI mistakes.
stories.audience: UK compliance, legal and HR teams, and anyone selling AI services into the UK.
stories.watch: The government’s reply to the Commons committee and whether an AI bill appears in the next King’s Speech.

source.title: UK Parliament, Joint Committee on Human Rights: Government response: Human Rights and the Regulation of AI, 20 November 2026
source.quote: We are not seeing a sense of urgency from the Government in addressing the serious risks that AI poses.

signals.raw: Scientific American, 20 Nov: Alpöge (Anthropic) claims Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis; Lean code independently compiled (Sutherland, MIT); comparator run pending (Buzzard). Nature: Granville calls the note garbled. TechCrunch: separate human proof by Masullo posted by Vakil, not in Lean.

Claude Help Center, 20 Nov: computer use beta for Team and Enterprise; off by default; Owner or Primary Owner enables; needs unified Chat and Cowork; macOS 14+ and Windows; not for HIPAA-ready, CMEK, FERPA/K-12, ZDR for Claude Code; no sandbox; screenshots saved with chat.

Anthropic, 20 Nov: IPO closed, 1,127,000,000 shares at $83 incl. 147M greenshoe; ~$93.5B gross, ~$91.6B to Anthropic; 313,253,007 Class N shares to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, TSMC for ~$26.0B; ~$119.5B total. Reuters: closed $88.91 Friday, -8.5%; ~$1.6T fully diluted.

Microsoft, 20 Nov: GPT-6.2 Sol rolling out in Copilot Chat, Cowork, Studio, Excel, PowerPoint, Word; Astra in Cowork and Studio, Frontier users in Chat and Office apps; Work IQ grounding within existing permissions.

OpenAI, 20 Nov: combatting adversarial distillation; reasoning-extraction attack success 54.0% (GPT-6 Astra) to 0.2% (GPT-6.2 Astra) in internal adaptive test; edited prefix drops later reasoning; older models cannot read 6.2 reasoning; closed pathway to another user’s encrypted reasoning.
